raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototypic angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), designed to inhibit maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone signaling while augmenting endogenous natriuretic peptide pathways. Its rationale emerged from the limitations of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition, which improved survival in HFrEF but left substantial residual risk [1]. Sacubitril is converted to sacubitrilat, which inhibits neprilysin, thereby increasing natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and other vasoactive substrates; valsartan counterbalances angiotensin II signaling, avoiding the excess angioedema observed with earlier dual ACE–neprilysin strategies while providing familiar ARB effects [2]. Pharmacologically, the combination lowers blood pressure, promotes natriuresis and cyclic guanosine monophosphate signaling, and may attenuate remodeling, fibrosis, and congestion [2,3].

The pivotal HFrEF evidence is PARADIGM-HF, in which sacubitril/valsartan was superior to enalapril in ambulatory patients with symptomatic HFrEF, reducing the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, and all-cause mortality [4]. Benefits were consistent in clinically important subgroups, including patients with recent decompensation and across baseline systolic blood pressure strata, although hypotension was more common and requires practical attention during initiation and titration [5,6]. Patient-centered benefits complemented hard outcomes: PARADIGM-HF demonstrated modest but durable improvements in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores [7]. Secondary analyses suggested favorable metabolic and biochemical effects, including improved glycemic control in diabetes and reduced uric acid, supporting the concept that ARNI therapy has systemic consequences beyond afterload reduction [8,9].

Implementation studies refined how to start therapy. TITRATION showed that gradual up-titration can improve tolerability, particularly among patients previously receiving low-dose or no ACE inhibitor/ARB [10]. TRANSITION demonstrated that starting sacubitril/valsartan before discharge or soon after discharge in stabilized HFrEF patients hospitalized for acute decompensation was feasible [11]. PIONEER-HF extended this evidence in hospitalized acute decompensated HFrEF: compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan produced a larger early NT-proBNP reduction without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [12]. Biomarker substudies showed parallel reductions in myocardial injury and wall-stress markers [13]. These data shifted ARNI from a “later switch” drug to a core component of early quadruple HFrEF therapy.

Mechanistic and remodeling data strengthen biologic plausibility. PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reductions after sacubitril/valsartan initiation with improvements in left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, left atrial volume, and diastolic indices [14]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant effect on aortic characteristic impedance but did show favorable changes in cardiac structure and biomarkers [15]. The PRIME trial suggested that ARNI may reduce functional mitral regurgitation more than valsartan in selected patients with LV dysfunction, consistent with reverse-remodeling effects [16]. In Japanese HFrEF patients, PARALLEL-HF supported broadly similar efficacy and safety to PARADIGM-HF, albeit with limited power for clinical events [17].

Evidence is more nuanced outside classic HFrEF. In PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan narrowly missed statistical significance for reducing total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death in patients with EF ≥45%, but signals were stronger at lower EF ranges and among women [18,19]. Renal analyses suggested slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate and fewer renal composite events than valsartan [20]. Pooled analyses across EF from PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF, and later PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF pooling, support a gradient of benefit that is greatest below normal EF and extends into mildly reduced EF [21,22]. Thus, ARNI is established in HFrEF, reasonable in HF with mildly reduced EF, and selectively useful in HFpEF phenotypes closer to the lower EF boundary.

Special populations require caution. PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce the primary composite after acute myocardial infarction compared with ramipril, so routine post-MI substitution is not established [23]. UK HARP-III found similar kidney function effects versus irbesartan in moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease, but advanced CKD and dialysis remain underrepresented in HF outcome trials [24]. LIFE, enrolling advanced HFrEF with recent NYHA class IV symptoms, did not show superiority over valsartan and highlighted tolerability constraints in severe disease; its run-in analysis underscores that hypotension, renal dysfunction, and hyperkalemia often limit initiation in advanced HF [25,26].

Current guidelines therefore place sacubitril/valsartan as foundational HFrEF disease-modifying therapy, ideally used with evidence-based beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors [27,28]. Practical prescribing requires a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors, avoidance in prior angioedema or pregnancy, dose adjustment for blood pressure, renal function, and potassium, and reassessment after hospitalization. Future work should clarify sequencing with other foundational drugs, benefits in EF-defined and phenotype-defined HFpEF, use in advanced kidney disease, and whether biomarker-guided or imaging-guided strategies can identify patients most likely to remodel favorably [29,30].
